beats.marks: Say nothing here. This is up while you're being introduced and getting settled. Do not talk over your own title card.

visual.title:
Mostly
not accounting.

a.lines:
B.S. Biomedical Engineering
B.A. Business Economics

b.lines:
7× Salesforce Certified (Advanced Admin)
3x CompTIA Certified (A+, Network+, Security+)
AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner
ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity and CISSP exam passed

visual.tail: No particular strategy, just a love of learning.

beats.opener: Before I get into anything, I want to point out the obvious here.
beats.rest:
A biomedical engineering degree from UC Irvine. Seven Salesforce certifications. A passed CISSP exam — among other things.

None of that is accounting.

I also double majored — business economics, same four years. Which, it turns out, had accounting classes in it. I couldn't have told you at the time why that mattered.

And I'll be honest about how those got picked. Biomedical engineering was my high school counselor's idea. Business economics I picked because it looked interesting. That's the whole strategy. There wasn't one.

I liked the math. Most of the rest I just got through. Nothing in school ever really grabbed me.

That happened at a job.
beats.marks: PAUSE two beats after "None of that is accounting" — hands still, let them agree with the objection. PAUSE again before "That happened at a job."

beats.opener: My first job out of college was in a lab doing cancer diagnostics. Mostly testing.
beats.rest:
Maybe an hour a day was entering results in an excel.

That hour was the part I liked. Not the typing — the spreadsheet. The validations, the formulas, the infinite chains of "if" statements until excel broke.

I was already trying to automate the job.
beats.marks: Last line lands better dry than wry. Don't push it.

visual.title:
They brought me in
for one project.
visual.sub: Years of historical preclinical data — structured differently based on a variety of things. A puzzle.

beats.opener: Somewhere in there I got good at Excel. Not impressively — just genuinely useful. Enough that people started bringing me things.
beats.rest:
And that's what got me to Amgen. They brought me in as a contractor for one project. Years of historical preclinical data — drug toxicology, pharmacology, real-time measurement — out of spreadsheets and into a real database. It is still the largest volume of data I have ever worked with.

And what made it hard wasn't the volume. No two of those spreadsheets were structured the same way. Same study, same measurements, completely different layouts — different people collected it over years, and every one of them had their own way of doing it. There was no standard, so everybody invented one.

So the program couldn't just move data. It had to read what somebody meant, not just what they typed, and land it in the same place every time.

That's the first time I understood what I actually liked. It wasn't the science. It was that the data was in the wrong shape — and nobody had done anything wrong. A lot of reasonable people had each just done it slightly differently.
beats.marks: Do NOT say this is what Vast is going through. Let it sit. It gets cashed in during Topic 2.

visual.title: I built the system with my previous experience in mind

items.lead: I volunteered to administer their Salesforce
items.sub: Six months later I was the department.
Sample intake · chain of custody · what has been run on what

items.lead: I'd used the big ones as a tech
items.sub: They're built for the person signing the purchase order — not the person at the bench with a sample in one hand and a barcode gun in the other.

visual.callout: And I could only build it because I'd been the one using it.

beats.cue: The accidental admin, and the build
beats.opener: Next was a CRO — a contract research organization. We collected and processed samples for other people's studies.
beats.rest:
They ran on Salesforce and needed somebody to administer it. I raised my hand, mostly out of curiosity.

The main thing I built there was a LIMS — laboratory information management system. Sample intake, chain of custody, where every sample is, what's been run on it.
beats.marks: The slide says "six months later I was the department" — let them read it, don't say it. Then let the callout land before moving on.

visual.title:
I keep automating
the job I just did.
visual.tail: Do the job by hand first. Feel exactly where it hurts. Then build the thing that makes it hurt less.

beats.opener: There's a pattern here, and I didn't notice it for years.
beats.rest:
I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

Every time, the sequence is identical. Do the job by hand first. Feel exactly where it hurts. Then build the thing that mitigates the pain point.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE, pass 1 of 3. Do NOT point forward to the 90-day plan — it gets paid off there, looking backward.

visual.title: Same move. Bigger.

items.sub: Project management built within Salesforce
Custom survey sends triggered by record statuses
Automated AR/AP payment sync, and a single source of truth

visual.callout: Eliminating pain points felt by myself and my colleagues.

beats.opener: Then ForensisGroup — an expert witness referral firm that ran its whole practice on Salesforce.
beats.rest:
Same move, bigger scale. I built PMify, project management for live cases. Survey Builder, a custom survey platform in Apex. And an automated AR/AP payment sync between Salesforce and QuickBooks.

That last one changed my life and I had no idea at the time. To build it I had to learn what actually happens to a payment. Not the button — the entry. What gets debited, what gets credited, and what breaks downstream if I get it wrong.

I was building accounting plumbing. And somewhere in there I noticed I cared more about what was moving through the pipe than about the pipe.
beats.marks: Slow down on "than about the pipe." That's the turn of the whole talk.

visual.title: I wanted skills that could help anyone.

items.sub: My third bachelor's degree.

items.lead: Enrolled Agent — admitted to practice before the IRS
items.sub: Business returns through Form 1120. Trial balance to Schedule L, book-to-tax on the M-1.
Completing the experience requirement.

visual.callout: Applying the skills throughout the days, nights, and even weekends.

beats.opener: So — why accounting. The real reason. I wanted a skill I could use on anybody.
beats.rest:
So I went and got the accounting degree at WGU. My third bachelor's.

Then I bought the CPA study materials, started in — and stopped. I went and passed the three Enrolled Agent exams first instead.

That was on purpose. The CPA is the longer road. The EA is the one that gets you hired to prepare returns. I wanted to be doing the work, not reading about it. So I took the detour, got admitted to practice before the IRS, and started preparing returns while I finished the rest. Books to returns is my normal commute.

Then all four CPA exams. I'm planning to sit for the CIA next.

And I'll be direct about why I did it this way. I don't have twenty years in accounting, and I'm not going to stand up here and imply I do. What I have is that I went and took every piece of it, deliberately, while working full time.
beats.marks: Last paragraph even and unhurried. It's a statement of fact, not a defence. CISSP stays on slide 2 — don't mention it here.

visual.title: Tax filing and auditing from the same books
visual.sub: Top performing tax preparer and sales & use tax auditor.

beats.opener: Which brings me to now. I'm a sales and use tax auditor for the State of California.
beats.rest:
The work is what it sounds like. I go into a business, I pull their records, and I test them. Capital equipment purchases are a standing part of what I test. So is use tax — which is the tax almost nobody self-reports correctly.

And here's the part I didn't expect. I spent a decade building the systems that produce these records. So now I open somebody's books and I can usually tell how an entry got made. Who made it. What screen they were looking at. Whether anyone ever looked at it again.
beats.marks: PAUSE before the last paragraph. This is the payoff of slide 2 — "none of this is accounting" turns out to be all of it.

beats.opener: Last thing before the topics. Outside of work I sing, and I play guitar. Sometimes both.
beats.rest: Til this day, I'm still trying to get on John Mayer's level.

visual.title:
Invoice came from
a repair vendor
visual.sub: A sales and use tax audit.

beats.opener: Topic one. Capitalize, or expense. Two calls — and for each one: what the rule wanted, what I did, how it came out, what I'd change.
beats.rest:
Quick thing first so it isn't sitting there. I've never kept a fixed asset subledger. What I've done is make this call from the return, from the audit, and on my own clients' books. The judgment I have. The posting is the part I'd learn.

First one's from a field audit, details disguised. People think a sales tax audit only looks at sales. It doesn't — we test what you bought too.

So I'm working the repairs and maintenance ledger. One vendor keeps showing up. Small amounts, a few hundred at a time. Compressor service, filter changes, booth maintenance. All consistent with the account.

Then one entry from that same vendor is twenty thousand dollars. Out-of-state, no tax charged. Equipment, freight, and installation on one invoice.

It's a spray booth. They bought the booth from the company that services their booths.
beats.marks: Say the bookkeeping line evenly and move — you're sizing it, not apologising. Slow on the last line.

a.lines:
Purchase price.
Installation labor is
excluded — Reg 1546.

b.lines:
Price plus freight
plus installation —
whatever it took to
get it working.

beats.opener: And this is the part of the job I actually like. That one invoice gets measured twice, two different ways.
beats.rest:
For my purposes, the use tax measure starts with the purchase price. But installation labor is excluded under Regulation 1546.

For their books, under ASC 360, it's the opposite instruction. Freight and installation go into the asset's basis, because basis is whatever it took to get it in place and working.

Same invoice. Two different numbers. Not because anyone's wrong — mine is asking what was purchased for use in California. Theirs is asking what the asset cost.
beats.marks: This is your credibility slide with the technical interviewer. Unhurried, and don't apologise for the detail.

visual.title: Expense or capitalize?

items.lead: The use tax was due either way
But it added capability and increased useful life

visual.callout: That same vendor's other invoices were genuine repairs. I left those alone.

beats.opener: Now, what did I actually decide? It's narrower than you'd think, and I want to be precise about it.
beats.rest:
The use tax didn't depend on the classification. Out-of-state tangible property, used in California, no tax paid to the vendor — use tax is due. Repair or asset, that doesn't move.

But the classification was wrong, and I raised it anyway, because it was their books. It added capability. They weren't fixing a booth, they were buying one. It lasts years. And it was expensed to repairs and never appeared on the depreciation schedule.

One more thing, and hold me to this. That same vendor's other invoices were real repairs. I left every one of them alone. If it only ever goes one way, it isn't judgment.
beats.marks: Say the repairs line plainly. The restraint is the point.

beats.opener: At the exit conference I walked the owner and their CPA through both pieces — what they owed, and separately, what their books had wrong. It held.
beats.rest:
And nobody was cheating. That's the part I keep coming back to.

The invoice sounded like a repair, so it went where repair invoices go, and it sat there for three years. Nobody ever revisited it.
beats.marks: Don't play this as a win. The next slide is why it matters.

visual.title:
The purchase
coded itself.
visual.sub: There was a rule. It was based on who sent the invoice, not what was on it.

beats.opener: Here's how it actually happened. That vendor was set up in their books with a default account, and the default was repairs and maintenance — because for years, that's all that vendor had ever sent them.
beats.rest:
The bill came in, it coded itself, and nobody overrode it.

So there was a rule. It was just keyed on who sent the invoice instead of what was on it.

And that's why it sat for three years. Additions to the depreciation schedule get reviewed — by their CPA, by their lender, by me. Costs buried in repairs don't get reviewed by anyone. The coding didn't create the liability. It hid it.

So that's what I'd change. Not the audit. The rule that coded it. Hold onto that.
beats.marks: "Keyed on who sent the invoice instead of what was on it" is the setup for the brilliant idea. Land it.

visual.title: Tax strategy consultation
visual.sub: Construction. S-corp. Keeps his own books.

a.lines:
$2,500 an invoice.
Expense it. No analysis.

b.lines:
Better, different, restored?
Capitalize. Pick a useful life.

beats.opener: Second one. Different chair. Nobody's books were on trial this time — somebody just asked me a question.
beats.rest:
Construction client of mine. Does fixer-uppers. He'd landed a contract bigger than anything he'd handled, and he wanted to know if he should elect S-corp.

And the honest answer wasn't about the election at all.
beats.marks: This is the slide that shows you advise on books. Don't rush it.

visual.title: Take it in the high year.
visual.sub: One contract. Income spikes, then drops back. A deduction is worth whatever rate you're in.

beats.opener: It was about what the election was going to cost him.
beats.rest:
Once his receipts or his assets cross two hundred fifty thousand, he's filing a Schedule L and an M-1. That's a real balance sheet, and a reconciliation between his books and his return.

Which means his books have to actually tie.

He was running a checkbook and a folder of receipts. That's a different business than the one he was asking about.

visual.title: He maintains the schedule.
visual.sub: Capitalize and every item needs a life and a class. No controller. No fixed asset system. Just him.

beats.opener: Then the equipment started coming. And now the call is mine, because I'm the one signing the return.
beats.rest:
Same test as the spray booth, different rulebook. Did it make the thing better, change what it does, or bring it back from broken? Any one of those and you capitalize it. None of them and it's a repair.

There's also a shortcut. The de minimis safe harbor lets you expense anything under twenty-five hundred an invoice and skip the analysis entirely.

But it has a condition. You need a written accounting policy, and it has to be in place before the tax year starts.

visual.title: The books and the return agree.
visual.sub: The election requires book conformity. So there is no book-to-tax difference to carry.

beats.opener: He didn't have one. So we couldn't use it.
beats.rest:
We capitalized a pile of small stuff that could have been deducted the day he bought it. Not because the rule said so — because nobody had written one paragraph the previous December.

And I'll own my part of that. He'd been my client the year before. I never told him to write it.
beats.marks: Flat. Don't soften it.

visual.title:
One found after.
One decided before.
visual.sub: Classify on purpose, at the source, in writing.

beats.opener: The lesson learned - you don't get to decide at the end of the year and justify it backwards. The policy must exist before the transaction does.
beats.rest:
Classify on purpose, at the source, in writing. That's not my opinion. That's the regulation.

Two calls. The first one had a rule — it was just keyed on the vendor instead of the invoice. The second one had no rule at all, because nobody wrote it. Including me.

I picked those two on purpose. I could have shown you two wins.

I did the job by hand, and I know exactly where it hurts. So let me tell you what I'd build.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE, pass 2. Straight into Topic 2 — no pause at the end.

visual.title:
I haven't done
international accounting.
visual.sub: I understand the concepts in theory. I just don't have the reps — yet.

beats.opener: Topic two. My first ninety days. And let me say the obvious part out loud, because you already know it. I haven't done international accounting.
beats.rest:
What I do have is the standards. FAR tested consolidation and currency translation — ASC 830, intercompany eliminations, the CTA running through OCI instead of income. I understand the concepts in theory. What I don't have is the reps.

But you've just watched me do this four times. I hadn't done data architecture, and I wrote the thing that moved it into a real database. I hadn't done Salesforce, and six months later I was the department. I hadn't done accounting at all, and I went and got a third bachelor's and passed four CPA exams.

I don't wait until I'm qualified. I go get qualified, and I do it while the work is happening.
beats.marks: PAUSE after "reps." Full stop. Don't rush to reassure — the silence is the confidence.

visual.title: Four things I'd have to practice.

items.sub: And whether it is translation at all, or remeasurement.
Intercompany, investment, minority interest
Set price charged for goods, services, or intellectual property exchanged between related business entities
Tokyo and Paris

visual.callout: My first question isn't how to book it. It's which determination was already made.

beats.opener: The terrain has four problems in it, and I already know their names.
beats.rest:
Currency translation under ASC 830 — yen and euro into dollars, with the translation adjustment running through OCI rather than income. Consolidation and eliminations. Transfer pricing — documentation that has to survive both Section 482 and a foreign authority looking at the same transaction from the other side.

And indirect tax. VAT and Japanese Consumption Tax. Which is the one I'd argue I already do — a reverse charge and California use tax are the same mechanism under different names. The seller doesn't collect, so the buyer self-assesses. I test that every working day.
beats.marks: Say the fourth one with a little more weight. It's the one place you're transferring, not learning.

visual.title: Do the job by hand.

items.lead: Walk one full closing cycle manually
items.sub: Japan's package through translation and eliminations, into the consolidated statements.

items.lead: Sit through one audit request cycle
items.sub: Not to fix anything. To see what gets asked for, and of whom.
Entities, currencies, elimination rules, subsidiary hierarchy.

visual.callout: Slowly, once, by hand. Know the current processes inside and out.

beats.opener: Month one: do the job by hand.
beats.rest:
I want to follow one close all the way through manually. Take Japan's reporting package, walk it through translation and eliminations, and land it in the consolidated statements. Once, by hand, slowly.

Not because that's efficient. Because that's the only way I've ever actually learned anything.

And I'll map how OneWorld is configured — what the system does automatically, versus what a person quietly fixes afterward.
beats.marks: You're deliberately echoing slide 6. Don't point at it — they'll feel it.

visual.title: Feel where it hurts.

items.lead: Own real close tasks, under review
items.sub: Reconciliations and translation entries that are mine.
Where do the hours go?

items.lead: Trace one PBC item end to end
items.sub: From the request to the document that satisfies it. How long did finding it take?

visual.callout: Identify possible KPIs that could be easily automated and reported.

beats.opener: Month two: feel where it hurts.
beats.rest:
By now I should be carrying real close tasks — reconciliations, translation entries — mine, under review by someone senior until that review stops being necessary.

And while I'm in there, I'm timing it. Where do the hours actually go? Most teams can't answer that, not because they're careless, but because nobody has ever had a reason to write it down.

Then I pick one automation with the controller. Highest pain, lowest risk. That's their call, not mine — I'm new.

visual.title: Build the thing that removes it.

items.lead: My slice of the close, fully owned
items.sub: No training wheels.
With a before-and-after number attached — not a claim, a measurement.

items.lead: Documented well enough to survive me
items.sub: If it only works while I'm in the room, I built a dependency.

beats.opener: Month three: build the thing that removes it.
beats.rest:
My slice of the close is fully mine by then, no training wheels. The first automation is live, with a before-and-after number attached — not a claim, a measurement.

And both documented well enough to survive me. If it only works while I'm in the room, I haven't actually finished it.

visual.title:
You've seen this
plan before.
visual.tail: It isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's the only way I've ever worked.

beats.opener: And I want to point at something.
beats.rest:
This is the same plan I've run my entire career. I did the bench work, then I built the lab system. I did the data entry, then I built the database.

So: I do your close by hand, I find out exactly where it hurts, and then I build the thing that takes it away.

That isn't a plan I wrote for this interview. It's the only way I've ever worked.
beats.marks: THROUGH-LINE, pass 3 of 3 — the payoff of slide 6. Let the third row of the diagram sit before you speak over it.

visual.title:
I built it before.
Substitute project with audit.
visual.sub: Supporting the audit came up as a pain point.
visual.tail: Every field already exists. Only the labels change.

beats.opener: So here's the one idea I was asked to bring. And it comes straight out of that spray booth.
beats.rest:
Ramp categorizes with AI. Most companies switch that on and treat it as a productivity feature.

But it isn't a feature. It's a control. Something is deciding what account a transaction lands in, thousands of times a month, and nothing is testing whether it was right.

If I walked into a business and asked what their detective control is over automated coding, most of them wouldn't have an answer.

So I'd build one.
beats.marks: "It's a control" is the sentence. Slow there. You audit the output of these systems — say it like someone who's seen it fail.

visual.title: PMify, pointed at the audit.

items.sub: Owner, due date, status, entity.
Not to an email thread. The answer lives with the question.
US, Japan, France — three statutory audits, three lists, one structure.
Who uploaded it, when, and who approved it. In security that's called non-repudiation.
This year's list is next year's starting point.

visual.callout: The second audit costs less than the first. The third costs less than the second.

beats.opener: Here's how it would have caught my spray booth, the day it landed.
beats.rest:
Three independent signals read the same invoice. The vendor default says repair, because that's what that vendor always sends. The amount says this is about fifty times that vendor's own median. The line items say equipment, freight, and installation.

Two of the three disagree with the default.

And that's the rule. You don't flag on any single signal — you flag when they disagree. Because the failure in my audit wasn't a bad rule. It was one rule, with nothing to check it against.

If they agree, it posts and nobody's day gets slower. If they disagree, it routes to a short review queue while somebody still remembers what it was for.
beats.marks: Let them make the Topic 1 connection before you spell it out. Say the last clause dry.

items.sub: Re-requests: how often the auditor has asked more than once. That's the quality number, not speed.

items.lead: Hours out of the close, not just moved
items.sub: Baseline the first cycle. Compare the second.
How much of this year's list survives.

items.lead: Evidence filed once, used three times
items.sub: Requests satisfied across US, Japan, and France from the same attachment — count the overlap.

beats.opener: And here's what would make it fail, because I'd rather say it than have you find it.
beats.rest:
A new vendor has no history, so there's nothing to compare against — those always go to review until there's a baseline. Below about five invoices the statistic is just noise, so it falls back to a flat threshold rather than pretending to know something.

One technical note. It compares against the median, not the average, because an average gets wrecked by exactly the outlier you're hunting for. One big purchase last year and the average stops flagging anything.

And the real risk isn't statistical, it's human. If it flags two hundred things a month everybody ignores it, and now you have something worse than no control — because people believe something is watching. So the threshold ties to materiality.

And it has to catch things wrongly capitalized too, not just wrongly expensed. Same discipline as the repairs I left alone.
beats.marks: This is the credibility slide. Naming the failure modes yourself is worth more than the idea. Unhurried.

visual.title:
I perform it.
Then improve it.
visual.sub: Requested, reviewed, approved, baselined, then implemented. Ninety days: close tasks owned · one automation live · improved audit support. Auditor's skepticism. Builder's toolkit.

beats.opener: I started by telling you I was the guy entering the data.
beats.rest:
Every job since, I did the work by hand first, found out where it hurt, and then built the thing that took it away. The lab system. The database. The payment sync. The audit chair.

So in ninety days: my close tasks owned. One automation live, with a real number on it. And a close that gets a step faster every month after that — because most closes never get faster, and it's not that anyone's bad at their job. Everybody owns their piece, their piece works, and nobody owns "faster."

I'm offering to own faster.

Thank you — I'd love your questions.
beats.marks: PAUSE before "I'm offering to own faster." Then land it, and STOP. Don't add a summary sentence.
